method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **SABA-only treatment is for mild, infrequent symptoms with no risk factors.** Frequent SABA alone (over 3 MDI canisters a year) with little preventer is associated with more severe exacerbations and death.
claims.source_text: Treatment with short-acting beta agonist (SABA) alone should only be used for children who have mild and infrequent symptoms with no risk factors … Frequent use of SABA alone (>3 MDI canisters per year) and infrequent use of preventer/anti-inflammatory is associated with more severe asthma exacerbation and death
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Diagnose on symptoms and treatment response** (clusters responding to SABA, or chronic symptoms responding to ICS) without red flags. **Red flags for another diagnosis:** productive or isolated cough, paraesthesia, chest pain, clubbing.
claims.source_text: Diagnosis is based on symptoms (wheeze, breathlessness, cough) and treatment response (ie recurrent clusters of symptoms that respond to SABA or chronic symptoms that respond to ICS) in the absence of red flags … Red flags for alternative diagnoses: productive cough isolated cough paraesthesia chest pain clubbing
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Exacerbation risk:** past intubation or ICU · 2 or more hospital presentations · SABA more than twice weekly or over 3 canisters a year · poor preventer adherence · poor technique · smoke/vaping exposure · obesity, sleep apnoea, chronic rhinosinusitis, confirmed food allergy.
claims.source_text: Risk of exacerbation History of intubation or intensive care unit (ICU) admission for asthma 2 or more presentations to hospital that require treatment for asthma Using SABA more than twice weekly or >3 MDI canisters per year Infrequent use/poor adherence of preventer/anti-inflammatory Incorrect inhaler technique Exposure to smoke/vaping Other comorbidities eg obesity, sleep apnoea, chronic rhinosinusitis, confirmed food allergy
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Good control:** daytime symptoms and reliever use less than two times a week, no activity limitation, night waking less than two times a month, no systemic steroid, ED visit or admission.
claims.source_text: Good asthma control is defined as: Daytime symptoms less than two times per week Need for reliever/SABA less than two times per week No limitation of activities Nighttime waking due to asthma less than two times per month No need for systemic corticosteroid, ED presentation or admission
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Look for contributors:** allergic rhinitis, obesity, sleep apnoea, reflux, dysfunctional breathing, depression/anxiety, smoking and vaping, damp or crowded housing.
claims.source_text: Consider contributing factors: Allergic rhinitis Obesity Obstructive sleep apnoea Gastro-oesophageal reflux Dysfunctional breathing (including vocal cord dysfunction) Depression/anxiety (may present as chest tightness without wheeze) Smoking and vaping (passive or active) Damp, mouldy, cold or crowded housing
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No investigations unless considering another diagnosis**; spirometry may help if diagnosis or severity is uncertain. **No allergy testing without a history of immediate reaction** to the allergen.
claims.source_text: No investigations are required unless considering an alternative diagnosis Spirometry may have a role in children in whom the diagnosis or severity is uncertain … Allergy testing (RAST/skin prick testing) should not be performed if there is no history of an immediate reaction to the potential allergen
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Every child gets salbutamol with a spacer: 100 microg MDI, 6–12 puffs** via spacer ± mask, carried at all times.
claims.source_text: SABA (salbutamol): all children should be prescribed SABA with spacer, and encouraged to have inhaler and spacer with them at all times Dose: salbutamol 100 microg MDI, 6 - 12 puffs (via spacer +/- mask)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Count canisters at each review — more than 3 a year is high risk.**
claims.source_text: Check number of canisters used between each review (>3 a year is high risk)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Step 1 — SABA only**, if no exacerbation treatment (systemic steroid or hospital) in 12 months, infrequent symptoms and no contributing factors. **Most other children need a preventer.**
claims.source_text: Step 1: SABA only Can use SABA only, without regular preventer, in children who have not required treatment for exacerbations (systemic corticosteroid or hospital presentation) in the past 12 months symptoms occur infrequently (see table below) no other contributing factors (smoking in household, obesity, social risk factors etc) Most other children require maintenance treatment (preventer)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Step 2 — low-dose ICS via spacer: ciclesonide 80 microg once daily or fluticasone 50 microg twice daily.** Ciclesonide: once daily, fewer side effects, PBS subsidised (not all spacers are compatible).
claims.source_text: Step 2: Low dose ICS via spacer (and reliever as needed) Ciclesonide 80 microg once daily or Fluticasone 50 microg twice daily … ciclesonide has the advantages of daily dosing, lower side effect profile, PBS subsidised so lower out of pocket costs (NB not all spacer devices are compatible)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Montelukast 5 mg once daily** is an alternative first-line preventer or ICS add-on — for steroid concerns or real difficulty with MDI + spacer.
claims.source_text: Montelukast can be used as an alternative first line preventer (or adjunct to ICS) in children requiring further control Montelukast 5 mg once daily … consider using as ICS alternative if significant parental concern regarding steroids or in children where use of MDI + spacer is particularly difficult
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **1 in 6 children on montelukast get agitation, sleep disturbance or mood change — stop it and see if they resolve.**
claims.source_text: 1 in 6 children may develop side effects with this medication including agitation, sleep disturbance and altered mood. If this occurs, cease medication to see if symptoms resolve
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Step 3 — moderate-dose ICS (fluticasone 100 microg twice daily or ciclesonide 160 microg once daily), OR low-dose ICS + montelukast, OR ICS/LABA:** budesonide/formoterol MDI 100/3 microg 2 puffs twice daily, or DPI 200/6 microg one inhalation twice daily.
claims.source_text: Step 3: Moderate dose ICS OR low dose ICS + montelukast OR ICS/LABA (and reliever as needed) Moderate dose ICS = fluticasone 100 microg twice daily or ciclesonide 160 microg once daily ICS/LABA = budesonide/formoterol MDI 100 microg/3 microg, 2 puffs twice daily or DPI 200 microg/6 microg, one inhalation twice daily
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Step 4 — moderate-dose ICS + montelukast, OR ICS/LABA + montelukast, OR refer for expert advice.**
claims.source_text: Step 4: moderate dose ICS + montelukast OR ICS/LABA + montelukast OR consider referring for expert advice.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Control:** good = all of daytime symptoms and reliever use ≤2 days a week, no activity limitation, no night symptoms; partial = one or two failing; poor = three or more. Pre-exercise reliever doses don't count.
claims.source_text: Good control (All of) Partial control (One or two of) Poor control (Three or more of) Daytime symptoms ≤2 days per week >2 days per week >2 days per week Need for reliever* ≤2 days per week >2 days per week >2 days per week Limitation to activity none present present Nighttime symptoms (or on waking) none present present … * Reliever frequency does not include doses taken prophylactically before exercise
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Start at Step 1 and step up after 6 weeks if needed — always check technique and adherence first**, and consider other diagnoses.
claims.source_text: Start at Step 1 and step up after 6 weeks if further control required Always check correct technique and adherence prior to stepping up. Consider alternate diagnoses
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **About 3 months of good control → consider stepping down.** Keep the lowest effective treatment; **cease only after 6 months symptom-free**, reviewing 4–6 weeks after each step down.
claims.source_text: Good control for a period of approximately 3 months suggest preventer treatment could be stepped down Continue the lowest treatment that controls symptoms Only cease treatment after a period of 6 months symptom-free and review 4-6 weeks after stepping down
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Nearing adolescence (10–11 years) with poor control: consider ICS-formoterol MART** — budesonide/formoterol DPI 200/6 microg (preferred with adequate technique) or MDI 100/3 microg; may be off-label or private script.
claims.source_text: For children who are nearing adolescence (ie 10-11 years old) and having difficulty with their asthma control, it is worth considering ICS-formoterol MART. … This can be prescribed as either budesonide/formoterol DPI (Turbuhaler®) 200 microg/6 microg or budesonide/formoterol MDI (Rapihaler®) 100 microg/3 microg DPI is preferred for those with adequate technique This may be prescribed “off label” or via private script
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Refer** if control is inadequate at Step 4 or the diagnosis is uncertain.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local paediatric team / respiratory or specialist asthma service when Inadequate asthma control achieved at Step 4 Diagnosis of asthma uncertain
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Annual influenza vaccine; check adherence every visit; a written asthma action plan for home and childcare.**
claims.source_text: Recommend annual influenza vaccine Check adherence at every visit and address barriers Asthma Action Plan: all children should have a written action plan for at home and childcare
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Many children can use a DPI from about age 6** — MDIs have a large carbon footprint; good control and switching to DPI reduce it.
claims.source_text: MDI have a large carbon footprint. The best way to decrease the impact is to achieve good asthma control to reduce need for SABA and/or switch to DPI when possible. Many children can generate adequate inspiratory pressure to use a DPI (from about age 6).
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not increase the ICS dose during an exacerbation** in a child already on daily ICS.
claims.source_text: In children already taking daily ICS, there is no role for increasing the dose of ICS during an exacerbation
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Asthma in primary school-aged children (6-11 years)' (Last updated June 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Asthma_in_primary_school-aged_children_(6-11_years)/, retrieved 2026-09-23
